content: The purpose of labour assessment programs is to delay hospital admission until the active phase of labour begins. This approach is intended to reduce unnecessary medical interventions for women who are not yet in established labour. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of these labour assessment programs compared to direct admission to labour wards. A search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group trials register as of January 2004. The review included randomized trials that compared labour assessment programs with direct admission to labour wards. The quality of the trials was carefully assessed. One high-quality study involving 209 women was included in the review. The findings showed that women who were assigned to the labour assessment unit spent significantly less time in the labour ward, with a weighted mean difference of 5.20 hours (95% confidence interval: -7.06 to -3.34). These women were also less likely to require intrapartum oxytocics, with an odds ratio of 0.45 (95% confidence interval: 0.25 to 0.80), and less likely to need analgesia, with an odds ratio of 0.36 (95% confidence interval: 0.16 to 0.78), compared to women who were admitted directly to the labour ward. Additionally, women in the labour assessment group reported feeling a greater sense of control during labour, with a weighted mean difference of 16.00 (95% confidence interval: 7.52 to 24.48). However, there was insufficient evidence to determine the effects of these programs on the rate of caesarean sections or other important maternal and neonatal outcomes. In conclusion, labour assessment programs designed to delay hospital admission until active labour may provide benefits for women with term pregnancies.
